items.title: PCA entry fee · ₱1,200 singles, pay first
items.detail: Official form says “No Pay, No Play”: men’s singles ₱1,200, doubles ₱900 each. Pay by BDO transfer to Philippine Columbian Association or QR-PH, then upload the receipt in the form. Easiest from LA: Wise to the BDO account shown on the form. Or Alex/Adelmo pays by QR-PH and you repay in cash. Check first whether “Sy, Jerry” (#159) is already your paid entry.

items.title: Philippines · set up GCash GTourist
items.detail: Locals pay by scanning GCash or Maya QR codes. GTourist is GCash for US visitors: sign up with your +1 number and passport (keep roaming on for the code). It activates once you land and lasts 30 days. Use up the balance before it ends.

items.title: Philippines · carry pesos
items.detail: Cash runs street food, small eateries, tricycles, tips and club courts. Apple Pay (live in PH since Aug 4, 2026) works at contactless terminals in malls, chains and hotels. ATMs charge foreign cards about ₱250 a withdrawal, so pull about ₱10,000 at a time and keep small bills. Grab and GrabFood take your US card.

items.title: Tokyo · Suica in Apple Wallet + ¥10,000–20,000 cash
items.detail: Wallet → + → Transit Card → Suica, top up with Apple Pay. No ID needed. It covers trains and convenience stores. Keep cash for small ramen counters, ticket-machine shops and izakayas; 7-Eleven ATMs take US cards. If one card fails to top up, try another.

items.title: Sending money to people in PH · Wise
items.detail: Wise sends dollars to pesos into a Philippine bank account or a GCash wallet. Use it for the PCA fee or paying back Alex or Adelmo.

items.title: Local SIM needs passport + address + onward ticket
items.detail: Philippine SIM registration asks for your passport, a local address (Adelmo’s works) and your ticket out. Tourist SIMs die after 30 days. An eSIM or US roaming skips this.

items.detail: Anthropic credit expires Nov 25: Muse’s balance check stopped at the platform.claude.com sign-in, so check it yourself. items.title: David Choe Lost in the Philippines (Thumbs Up Season 5)
items.detail: Choe's whole Philippines method is to put the phone away, say yes to whoever talks to you and let the day lead, and it gives Jerry a ready list of stops: Quiapo Church and its palm readers, Greenhills for bootleg toys and 30-peso Pokemon packs, then Siargao for a boat trip to Ma'mon Island, lechon, Bebe's Barbeque and Mrs. Krispy fried chicken. Why: In Manila Jerry can do Choe's Quiapo Church stop (palm readers and the Black Nazarene) and Greenhills Shopping Center (bootleg toys and cheap Pokemon packs; the street fruit and haggling scenes are not located on screen) around PCA Open match days; if he adds Siargao instead of or after Cebu, Choe's day was island hopping by boat to Ma'mon Island, jet skis at sunset, a lechon pig face, Bebe's Barbeque with its house band, and Mrs. Krispy fried chicken, plus a warning that he got traveler's diarrhea there. Contact: Quiapo Church, Instagram @quiapochurch (https://www.instagram.com/quiapochurch/), 910 Plaza Miranda, Quiapo, Manila, site quiapochurch.com.ph; Greenhills Mall, Instagram @greenhillsph (https://www.instagram.com/greenhillsph/), Ortigas Avenue, Greenhills, San Juan. Bebe's Barbeque and Mrs. Krispy in Siargao had no Instagram I could verify; go in person. Bobby Trivia's account was not verified.

items.title: David Choe Painting in the Philippines
items.detail: This is a mostly wordless painting livestream in which Choe, working with unfamiliar local brushes, acrylics and a loose, thrice-painted canvas, adapts instead of complaining and breaks to rip open Pokemon packs on chat's urging. Why: It has little travel value: no place in Manila or Siargao is named, so it is only worth watching for Choe's mindset (adapt to whatever gear and conditions the country gives you, which applies to unfamiliar courts and balls at the PCA Open) and for his Pokemon card habit, which the full episode ties to Greenhills. The shop visit is the easiest first meeting of the trip. items.title: UNDERCOVER Jun Takahashi Interview
items.detail: In the only clearly captioned talk, Jun Takahashi explains UNDERCOVER's PCM temperature-regulating fabric and says an exhibition (instead of a runway show) let him go back and deepen older functional ideas rather than chase new ones. Why: Jun is on Tom's Tokyo designer list, and this gives Tom a specific making topic (functional fabric that stores and releases body heat, revisited from a 2007 winter collection) to raise instead of a generic compliment. Most of the video is music or uncaptioned Japanese, so treat it as light background. items.title: UNDERCOVER Jun Takahashi interview at The Corner
items.detail: Jun Takahashi says function and current technology must go into the clothes he wears and took Dieter Rams's "less but better" as his theme: cut out waste and do what you can. Why: Jun's push toward function, comfort and technology, with minimal waste, is the language Tom will use to describe tennis gear, so this gives him a shared design principle to raise with UNDERCOVER's team. items.title: UNDERCOVER A/W 1997-98 "Leaf": Behind the Scenes (TV excerpt)
items.detail: Jun Takahashi built UNDERCOVER by starting from copying, casting friends who "do what they love," and treating music as raw material, and his advice to young makers is simply that you have to do it. Why: This 1997 Japanese TV segment shows how Jun ran UNDERCOVER as a small Harajuku label with friends, shop builders and musicians, which is the closest model to Tom's own small tennis bandana and clothing line and gives him real history to open a conversation with in Tokyo. items.title: UNDERCOVER 35th Anniversary Feature "but beautiful 4...": Behind the Scenes, 2025.1.25 to 3.4, Tokyo chapter
items.detail: Jun Takahashi's method is to take something everyone finds cute, like a teddy bear, add one "spice," then strip details until people can still recognize it, because "if people can't tell what it is, it doesn't communicate." Why: This is UNDERCOVER's own film of its Harajuku atelier and Tokyo makers finishing a Paris collection, so it shows Tom exactly how Jun's team works with craftspeople, how far ahead they finish pieces, and what they value in makers ("nothing but love"). Why: For a small brand like Tom's, this shows that Tokyo's street founders judge clothes by everyday wearability plus the wording and graphics on them, which is the angle Tom's bandanas and tees can lead with when he meets them. items.title: Nike x Undercover GYAKUSOU, Spring 2011: Behind the Scenes with Jun Takahashi

items.title: KREVA visits the ALMOSTBLACK atelier: inside the special collaboration and the deep side of making clothes (【KREVAが訪問】ブランドALMOSTBLACKのアトリエに潜入！特別コラボの裏側と服作りのディープな裏側を探る)

items.detail: Yuichi Shibui is a graphic designer and avid runner, not a trained clothing designer, who built a one-person, all made-in-Japan running brand by mixing vintage and street taste with top technical fabrics, which is close to what Tom is trying to do with tennis. Why: Shibui is the clearest model in Tokyo for a sport-first apparel brand run by one person with Japanese factories, and he says he got his first big collaboration (Joe Grant) because someone noticed the product on a run. Tom can open with running and his bandanas, and ask about Japanese factories, minimums and Polartec-style fabric access.
